title: Your own experiment
hookLine: try a practice for a month and track how you feel

lines: A BLACK SPOT FOR EACH SLIP.
cards: A printer in Philadelphia buys a small notebook. On each page he writes one virtue he wants to grow into, and rules the page into a grid of days.

Every evening he looks back and marks a small black spot wherever he fell short. The printer is Benjamin Franklin, telling this story himself in his autobiography. He's running an experiment with one subject: himself.
After weeks of other people's studies, the lab is yours.

teach.h: A LITTLE BOOK, A PAGE PER VIRTUE.
teach.b: First, Franklin's method. In his words: "I made a little book, in which I allotted a page for each of the virtues."

He gave his attention to one virtue at a time and kept score honestly, spots and all, and he admits the book filled with more faults than he'd expected. Second, why a personal experiment is worth doing.
Studies tell us what tends to happen across many people.
They can't tell you what a practice does in your life, with your schedule and your temperament. A month of careful trying can. Third, the honest limits.

teach.h: NO CONTROL GROUP; HOPES COLOR IT.
teach.b: An experiment of one has no comparison group.

teach.h: ONE PRACTICE, ONE MEASURE, ONE MONTH.
teach.b: Hopes shape what we notice; if you expect a practice to help, you may rate your days a little kinder. And life moves on its own: a hard week at work can swamp any practice. So keep it simple.

One practice. A measure decided before you start, maybe a one-to-five rating of mood or sleep each night, written at the same time every day. At the end, look at the whole month, not just the best day or the worst.
Fourth, what you're really testing. Not whether a practice is true. Whether it helps you, here, now, and what it costs you.
Franklin didn't become perfect. He said the attempt made him better and happier than he otherwise would have been. A modest finding, and the kind a person can actually use.

how: Some people test a practice on themselves for a month, choosing one simple daily rating before they start and reading the whole month at the end, much as Benjamin Franklin kept a little book of his virtues.

o: testing whether a religion's teachings are true
one practice, one measure, tracked honestly for a month
a lab study you sign up for at a nearby university

games.q: you're starting a month-long test of a practice. when should you decide what you'll track?
o: at the end, once you see what changed.
before you start, and write it down.
games.why: deciding first keeps you honest. picking the measure afterward lets you find whatever you hoped to find.

practice: Let one practice from this path come forward, the one you're most curious about: two hours outside, the slow breath, a mental photograph of a good moment, coaching yourself by name.
Settle on that one, and on one number each night, one to five, for mood, sleep or calm. If you pray, you can offer the month as an intention.

wordCard.voice: Your own experiment. One practice, one simple measure, one month, read honestly, knowing hopes can color the results. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my experiment. Kept honestly, spots and all, the way Franklin kept his. Rest well.
